questions.stem: A 44 year old man has 2 months of itching around the anus and mucus staining his underwear. He sees bright red blood coating his stool and on the paper, and often feels he has not fully emptied. There is no pain, weight loss or change in bowel habit. He feels well and his abdomen is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Painless bright red blood coating the stool, pruritus from mucus leakage and a sense of incomplete emptying in a well patient is internal haemorrhoids.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: bright red blood coating his stool
steps.x: Painless bright red bleeding plus mucus and itch, with no systemic symptoms = internal haemorrhoids.

elim: A fissure causes sharp pain on defecation, which he does not have.
A fistula discharges pus or blood from an external opening and follows an abscess.
He has no weight loss, change in bowel habit or systemic upset.
Threadworms cause nocturnal itch, mostly in children, without bleeding.

steps.x: C: Internal haemorrhoids. Internal haemorrhoids sit above the dentate line and are usually painless.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman has painless bright red blood on the toilet paper after opening her bowels. She has never felt or seen a lump, even when straining. Proctoscopy shows enlarged vascular cushions above the dentate line that do not prolapse when she strains.
questions.q: Which is the grade of her haemorrhoids?
questions.e: Haemorrhoids that bleed but never protrude are grade 1.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the grade of her haemorrhoids? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: never felt or seen a lump
do not prolapse when she strains
steps.x: Grade by prolapse: none, reduces itself, needs pushing back, stays out.

elim: Grade 2 protrudes on straining and reduces spontaneously.
Grade 3 protrudes and needs manual reduction.
Grade 4 is permanently prolapsed.
This is a painful purple lump at the anal margin.

steps.x: A: Grade 1. Grade 1: no protrusion.

questions.stem: A 47 year old lorry driver has painless bright red bleeding after defecation. He notices a soft lump coming out of his anus when he strains, which slips back inside on its own within a few minutes. He has no pain, weight loss or change in bowel habit.
questions.q: Which is the grade of his haemorrhoids?
questions.e: Haemorrhoids that protrude on straining and reduce spontaneously are grade 2.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the grade of his haemorrhoids? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: slips back inside on its own
steps.x: Reduces by itself = grade 2; needs a finger = grade 3.

elim: Grade 1 does not protrude at all.
Grade 3 needs manual reduction.
Grade 4 cannot be reduced.
Full-thickness prolapse is larger, has concentric folds and usually needs pushing back.

steps.x: B: Grade 2. Grade 2: protrudes on straining, reduces spontaneously.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman has had haemorrhoids for many years. For the last 6 months a lump has stayed outside her anus all the time. She has tried pushing it back but it will not stay in or go back at all. It bleeds and makes hygiene difficult. It is not acutely painful.
questions.q: Which is the grade of her haemorrhoids?
questions.e: Permanently prolapsed haemorrhoids that cannot be reduced are grade 4.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the grade of her haemorrhoids? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: stayed outside her anus all the time
will not stay in or go back at all
steps.x: Irreducible = grade 4.

elim: Grade 1 does not protrude.
Grade 2 reduces spontaneously.
Grade 3 can still be pushed back manually.
A haematoma is an acute, painful, small purple lump.

steps.x: D: Grade 4. Grade 3 needs manual reduction; grade 4 is permanently prolapsed and irreducible.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman is 3 days after a vaginal delivery with a long second stage of pushing. She has sudden, severe anal pain that makes it hard to sit. Her temperature is 36.9°C and pulse rate 88 bpm. Before this she had soft, painless swellings at the anal margin during pregnancy.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Purple, tense, very tender anal lump
questions.e: Sudden severe anal pain with a purple, oedematous, very tender lump at the anal margin is a thrombosed external haemorrhoid; pushing in labour is a classic trigger.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on examination? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: soft, painless swellings at the anal margin
steps.x: Sudden pain plus a lump after straining = thrombosis.

elim: This describes a perianal abscess; she is afebrile.
Severe pain this sudden will have a visible cause.
Uncomplicated internal haemorrhoids are painless.
A fissure gives pain on defecation, not constant pain with a lump.

steps.x: E: Purple, tense, very tender anal lump. Thrombosed haemorrhoid: sudden severe pain, purple oedematous tender lump.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man has 3 months of painless bright red bleeding and a lump that prolapses on straining and reduces by itself. He has a BMI of 34, works lifting heavy boxes and passes hard stools every 4 days. He eats very little fibre and has no family history of bowel disease.
questions.q: Which is the most important contributing factor?
questions.e: Constipation and straining raise intra-anal pressure and engorge the vascular cushions; obesity, heavy lifting and a low-fibre diet add to it.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most important contributing factor? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Anything that raises intra-abdominal pressure engorges the cushions; straining is the main one.

elim: He has none, and haemorrhoids are not inherited this way.
Protein is not the issue; low fibre is.
Systemic blood pressure does not cause haemorrhoids.
Exercise is protective against constipation.

steps.x: A: Chronic straining with constipation. Causes: constipation, straining, pregnancy, obesity, low-fibre diet.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman with alcohol-related cirrhosis, ascites and splenomegaly has painless bright red blood on the paper after defecation. She has no haematemesis or melaena. Proctoscopy shows engorged vascular cushions above the dentate line at 3, 7 and 11 o'clock.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Engorged cushions at the classic 3, 7 and 11 o'clock positions are internal haemorrhoids; chronic liver disease worsens them because portal hypertension raises pressure in the haemorrhoidal plexus, a different mechanism from oesophageal varices.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Cushions in the classic positions are haemorrhoids, made worse by portal hypertension.

elim: There is no pain and no tear.
Varices give haematemesis and melaena, not bright red blood on the paper.
HCC does not cause rectal bleeding.
UC gives bloody diarrhoea, not cushions at 3, 7 and 11 o'clock.

steps.x: D: Internal haemorrhoids. Chronic liver disease worsens haemorrhoids via raised venous pressure in the haemorrhoidal plexus.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman with known haemorrhoids has 12 hours of severe anal pain. The haemorrhoids prolapsed during defecation and she cannot push them back. Her temperature is 37.6°C and pulse rate 98 bpm. Examination shows tense, dark purple, oedematous prolapsed haemorrhoids with an area of ulceration.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Prolapsed internal haemorrhoids that cannot be reduced become oedematous, thrombosed and ulcerated: strangulation, which needs urgent surgical review.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Irreducible, dusky and ulcerated = strangulated.

elim: Cancer is not acute, painful and dusky over 12 hours.
Grade 2 reduce spontaneously and are painless.
An abscess is a red fluctuant swelling, not prolapsed purple cushions.
Full-thickness prolapse is usually painless with concentric mucosal folds.

steps.x: E: Strangulated prolapsed haemorrhoids. Complications: anaemia, thrombosis, ulceration, pain, prolapse; strangulation is urgent.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has soft, itchy, skin-covered swellings around her anus that make cleaning difficult. They are not painful and rarely bleed. On inspection and digital rectal examination there are soft, compressible perianal lumps arising below the dentate line, covered by skin.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Skin-covered, compressible perianal swellings below the dentate line, felt on DRE, are external haemorrhoids; they become painful if thrombosed.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: below the dentate line, covered by skin
steps.x: Below the dentate line and skin-covered = external.

elim: Warts are cauliflower-like papules, not soft compressible cushions.
Grade 1 internal haemorrhoids are not seen or felt externally.
Pilonidal disease is in the natal cleft, not perianal.
Prolapse is mucosa from above, not skin-covered lumps below the dentate line.

steps.x: B: External haemorrhoids. External haemorrhoids: below the dentate line, positive DRE, painful if thrombosed.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman has 6 weeks of painless bright red blood dripping into the pan after defecation. She has never noticed a lump. She has no weight loss or change in bowel habit. Her abdomen is soft. A digital rectal examination is performed before proctoscopy.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on digital rectal examination?
o: Tender purple lump at the anal margin
questions.e: Internal haemorrhoids are soft vascular cushions that sit higher and may not prolapse, so DRE is often normal; proctoscopy shows them.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on digital rectal examination? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Soft cushions collapse under the finger; you see them, not feel them.

elim: This suggests rectal cancer, which does not fit a painless, well 39 year old.
A fissure is very painful and she has no pain.
Impaction does not cause bright red dripping blood.
That is a thrombosed external haemorrhoid, which is painful.

steps.x: B: No abnormality felt. Internal haemorrhoids may give a negative DRE; external usually give a positive DRE.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man has 24 hours of sudden severe anal pain that started after lifting heavy weights at the gym. He has a 1 cm tender lump at the anal verge. He has no fever. His bowel habit is normal and he has no bleeding.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of the lump?
questions.e: Sudden severe anal pain with a small tender lump at the margin after straining is a thrombosed external haemorrhoid (purple, oedematous, very tender).

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of the lump? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: 1 cm tender lump at the anal verge
steps.x: Sudden onset after straining with a tender lump = thrombosis.

elim: A fissure is a tear with pain on defecation, not a lump.
Internal haemorrhoids are painless unless strangulated.
An abscess develops over days with fever and fluctuance.
Pilonidal disease is in the natal cleft.

steps.x: E: Thrombosed external haemorrhoid. Thrombosed haemorrhoid: sudden severe pain and a tender lump on the anal margin.

questions.stem: A 54 year old man has 8 months of near-daily painless bright red bleeding from known grade 2 haemorrhoids. He now has fatigue and breathlessness on stairs. Colonoscopy shows no other source of bleeding.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for his blood results?
questions.e: Chronic bleeding from haemorrhoids can cause iron-deficiency anaemia; colonoscopy has excluded other causes.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely explanation for his blood results? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Low MCV and ferritin with chronic visible bleeding and a clear colon = haemorrhoidal blood loss.

elim: Ferritin is low and MCV is low, so this is iron deficiency.
Coeliac disease is a cause of iron deficiency but he has an obvious bleeding source.
Colonoscopy has excluded another bleeding source.
B12 deficiency gives a high MCV.

steps.x: B: Chronic haemorrhoidal blood loss. Complications: anaemia from chronic bleeding, thrombosis, ulceration, pain, prolapse.

questions.stem: A 31 year old man has painless bright red blood on the paper. He notices a lump on straining that goes back by itself. He has no weight loss, change in bowel habit or family history. On inspection with straining, soft pink swellings appear at the anal verge and then reduce.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate way to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Haemorrhoids are a clinical diagnosis, with proctoscopy if needed; here they are visible on straining in a young patient with no red flags.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate way to confirm the diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: no weight loss, change in bowel habit or family history
steps.x: Seen on examination, no red flags: the diagnosis is clinical.

elim: Barium studies have no role in diagnosing haemorrhoids.
Colonoscopy is for red flags or diagnostic uncertainty.
CT does not diagnose haemorrhoids.
MRI is for fistulas and rectal cancer staging.

steps.x: B: Clinical examination alone. Gold standard: clinical diagnosis, with proctoscopy if needed.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman with known grade 1 haemorrhoids has had 3 months of bleeding despite fibre and topical treatment. The blood is now sometimes darker and mixed with stool, and her stools have become looser. She has no weight loss. Proctoscopy shows small haemorrhoids only.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Diagnostic uncertainty or red flags (darker blood mixed in, change in bowel habit) need flexible sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy to exclude proximal pathology.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next investigation? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Symptoms not explained by small haemorrhoids = look higher.

elim: A plain film does not show mucosal disease.
Anal ultrasound looks at the sphincters.
Darker blood mixed in and a change in stool needs endoscopy.
Delay risks missing a proximal cause.

steps.x: C: Flexible sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy. Second-line: flexible sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy for uncertainty or red flags.

questions.stem: A 37 year old man has 4 weeks of painless bright red bleeding after defecation. He has no pain, weight loss or change in bowel habit. External inspection of the anus is normal and digital rectal examination is unremarkable.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: A normal DRE does not exclude internal haemorrhoids, which sit higher and may not prolapse; proctoscopy shows them directly.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate investigation? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Normal DRE + typical bleeding = look with a proctoscope.

elim: There are no red flags in a young man with typical bleeding.
CT is not used to find haemorrhoids.
Calprotectin is for suspected IBD with diarrhoea.
MRI is not used to diagnose haemorrhoids.

steps.x: E: Proctoscopy. Clinical diagnosis with proctoscopy if needed.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman has 6 months of near-daily painless bright red bleeding from proctoscopy-confirmed grade 3 haemorrhoids. She has become tired and short of breath on exertion. She has no weight loss and her bowel habit is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Tiredness and breathlessness after months of bleeding suggest iron-deficiency anaemia, a complication of chronic haemorrhoidal bleeding; check an FBC first.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Chronic bleeding plus fatigue: check for anaemia.

elim: Manometry assesses continence, not blood loss.
CEA is a colorectal cancer monitoring marker.
There is no suggestion of a bleeding disorder.
LFTs do not assess blood loss.

steps.x: D: Full blood count. Complication: anaemia from chronic bleeding.

questions.stem: A 35 year old man has 4 weeks of painless bright red bleeding after defecation. Proctoscopy shows non-prolapsing haemorrhoids. He eats very little fruit or vegetables and strains to pass hard stools. He has no red flags and has not had any treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: First-line management is a high-fibre, high-fluid diet and avoiding straining, with a bulk-forming laxative such as ispaghula husk for symptom relief.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Untreated, low fibre and straining: fix the stool first.

elim: Surgery is for grade 3 to 4 or failed treatment.
Sclerotherapy is not used before conservative measures.
Codeine is constipating and worsens straining.
Banding is for persistent haemorrhoids after conservative treatment.

steps.x: B: Increase dietary fibre and fluids. First-line: fibre, fluids, avoid straining, ispaghula husk.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman has grade 1 haemorrhoids that still bleed and itch after 6 weeks of a high-fibre diet and ispaghula husk. She is not pregnant. She would like to avoid any procedure.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next treatment?
questions.e: For grade 1 haemorrhoids, the definitive treatment in the notes is topical hydrocortisone; it is contraindicated in pregnancy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next treatment? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Grade 1, not pregnant, wants no procedure = topical steroid.

elim: Surgery is for severe grade 3 to 4 disease.
Antibiotics have no role in uncomplicated haemorrhoids.
This is an operation for prolapsing disease.
GTN treats anal fissures.

steps.x: E: Topical hydrocortisone. Grade 1: topical hydrocortisone (not in pregnancy).

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman who is 34 weeks pregnant has itchy, uncomfortable haemorrhoids that bleed a little after defecation. She already drinks plenty of water and eats a high-fibre diet. She asks for a cream to soothe the area.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate topical treatment?
questions.e: In pregnancy a topical emollient such as Anusol is used with fibre and fluids; hydrocortisone is avoided.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate topical treatment? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Pregnant: emollient yes, steroid no.

elim: GTN is for fissures and causes headaches.
Topical hydrocortisone is contraindicated in pregnancy.
This is not a treatment for haemorrhoids.
This is an eczema treatment.

steps.x: A: Topical emollient (Anusol). Pregnancy: fibre, fluids, topical emollient (Anusol).

questions.stem: A 38 year old man has grade 2 haemorrhoids that make the anus sore for an hour after each bowel motion. He has just started a high-fibre diet and ispaghula husk. He wants something to ease the soreness while these take effect.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment for his symptoms?
questions.e: Topical creams and local anaesthetic preparations relieve symptoms while conservative measures take effect; opioids should be avoided.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate treatment for his symptoms? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Symptom relief without constipating him = topical anaesthetic.

elim: Surgery is not indicated for grade 2 disease at this stage.
Codeine is constipating and worsens straining.
Antibiotics do not help haemorrhoids.
Banding is for persistent symptoms after conservative treatment.

steps.x: E: Topical local anaesthetic. First-line includes topical creams or local anaesthetic.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman has grade 2 haemorrhoids that still bleed and prolapse after 3 months of a high-fibre diet, fluids, ispaghula husk and topical treatment. She has no red flags. She is keen on a clinic procedure rather than an operation.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Persistent grade 1 to 3 haemorrhoids after conservative treatment are treated with rubber band ligation via an anoscope in clinic; sclerotherapy, infrared photocoagulation and stapled haemorrhoidopexy are alternatives.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: clinic procedure rather than an operation
steps.x: Failed conservative, grade 1 to 3 = banding.

elim: Symptoms persist after an adequate trial.
Surgery is reserved for severe grade 3 to 4 disease.
This is an operation for chronic anal fissure.
GTN is a fissure treatment.

steps.x: D: Rubber band ligation. Second-line: rubber band ligation.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man has grade 3 haemorrhoids that he has to push back after every bowel motion. They have been banded twice in the past year and still bleed and prolapse. He has no red flags and is fit for surgery.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Severe grade 3 to 4 haemorrhoids, especially after failed banding, are treated by haemorrhoidectomy; sclerotherapy and infrared coagulation are only adjuncts.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Recurrent grade 3 after banding = operation.

elim: Banding has failed twice.
Conservative treatment cannot fix recurrent grade 3 disease.
This is for anal fissure.
Topical steroid is for grade 1 disease.

steps.x: B: Haemorrhoidectomy. Gold standard for severe grade 3/4: haemorrhoidectomy.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman has 36 hours of excruciating anal pain from a 2 cm purple, tense, thrombosed external haemorrhoid. Despite regular paracetamol, ibuprofen, ice packs and stool softeners she cannot sit or sleep. She has no fever.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Thrombosed haemorrhoids are treated with analgesia, stool softeners and ice packs; excision is used if the pain is severe despite this.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: Despite regular paracetamol, ibuprofen, ice packs and stool softeners
steps.x: Conservative treatment has failed and pain is severe: excise.

elim: There is no infection.
Banding below the dentate line is extremely painful and is not used for external haemorrhoids.
This is for prolapsing internal haemorrhoids.
Steroid cream will not relieve a tense thrombus.

steps.x: A: Excision of the thrombosed haemorrhoid. Thrombosed haemorrhoid: analgesia, softeners, ice; excision if severe.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man on apixaban for atrial fibrillation has 6 hours of heavy bright red bleeding from known haemorrhoids, filling the pan with clots. His pulse rate is 116 bpm and BP 96/60 mmHg. He feels dizzy on standing.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Increase fibre and review in 2 weeks
questions.e: Severe bleeding, thrombosis or strangulation need urgent review; this patient is tachycardic and hypotensive and needs resuscitation and urgent assessment.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Shocked from rectal bleeding = emergency, whatever the cause.

elim: He is haemodynamically unstable.
This ignores active, severe bleeding.
Creams do not treat haemodynamically significant bleeding.
Laxatives do not stop major bleeding.

steps.x: E: Urgent hospital assessment and resuscitation. Severe bleeding, thrombosis or strangulation need urgent review.

questions.stem: A 25 year old medical student asks why everyone has haemorrhoidal tissue if haemorrhoids are a disease. Her tutor explains that the anal canal contains normal vascular cushions made of arteriovenous connections and connective tissue.
questions.q: Which is the main normal function of these cushions?
o: Help with fine control of continence
questions.e: Haemorrhoids are dilated versions of normal anal vascular cushions, which help seal the anal canal and control stool.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the main normal function of these cushions? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Cushions fill with blood to plug the canal.

elim: Water absorption happens in the colon.
Mucus comes from goblet cells, not vascular cushions.
Tone comes from the internal and external sphincters.
Rectal filling is sensed by stretch receptors in the rectal wall.

steps.x: B: Help with fine control of continence. Haemorrhoids are dilated vascular cushions that normally help with stool control.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman is 32 weeks pregnant and has been constipated for months. She develops painless bleeding and a prolapsing lump on straining. Her midwife explains how pregnancy and constipation lead to her symptoms.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Autoimmune inflammation of the rectal mucosa
Raised pressure engorging the anal cushions
questions.e: Raised intra-abdominal and intra-anal pressure from straining, constipation and the pregnant uterus makes the normal cushions abnormally engorged and prolapsed.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Pressure from above plus straining = engorged cushions.

elim: That describes proctitis.
That is the cause of Hirschsprung's disease.
This causes perianal abscess and fistula.
That is an anal fissure, which is painful.

steps.x: D: Raised pressure engorging the anal cushions. Haemorrhoids: normal cushions engorged by raised intra-abdominal/intra-anal pressure.

questions.stem: A 31 year old man has a thrombosed external haemorrhoid. He asks why it is so painful when his friend's internal haemorrhoids bled for months without any pain.
questions.q: Which best explains the pain of his haemorrhoid?
o: Somatic innervation below the dentate line
Spasm of the internal sphincter only
Visceral innervation of the anal canal
questions.e: External haemorrhoids lie below the dentate line under somatically innervated squamous epithelium (inferior rectal nerve), so they are painful, especially when thrombosed.

steps.x: The question asks: Which best explains the pain of his haemorrhoid? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Below the dentate line = somatic = pain.

elim: Columnar mucosa lies above the dentate line and is insensate.
Thrombosis, not infection, causes this pain.
Sphincter spasm is the main pain source in fissures.
Visceral innervation above the dentate line makes internal haemorrhoids painless.

steps.x: C: Somatic innervation below the dentate line. Internal: above dentate line, visceral, painless; external: below, somatic, painful.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman has painless bleeding from internal haemorrhoids. A biopsy taken by mistake during proctoscopy from the surface of one cushion is sent to histology. It came from above the dentate line.
questions.q: Which epithelium is most likely to be seen?
questions.e: Internal haemorrhoids lie above the dentate line, covered by insensate columnar or transitional mucosa with visceral innervation, which is why they are painless.

steps.x: The question asks: Which epithelium is most likely to be seen? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Above the dentate line = gut-type mucosa.

elim: This lines the airways.
This is perianal skin below the dentate line.
This lines ducts and kidney tubules.
Urothelium lines the bladder.

steps.x: B: Columnar or transitional mucosa. Internal haemorrhoids: columnar/transitional mucosa, visceral nerves, painless.

questions.stem: A 51 year old man has rubber band ligation of grade 2 internal haemorrhoids. He is told that the treated haemorrhoid will fall off within about a week and he may notice a little blood when it does.
questions.q: Which is the mechanism by which banding works?
questions.e: A tight band cuts off the blood supply, causing ischaemic necrosis and fibrosis; the haemorrhoid sloughs off and the scar fixes the mucosa.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the mechanism by which banding works? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: fall off within about a week
steps.x: Band = no blood = dead tissue drops off.

elim: That is how injection sclerotherapy works.
That is infrared photocoagulation.
That is how GTN and diltiazem treat fissures.
That is a haemorrhoidectomy.

steps.x: C: Ischaemic necrosis then sloughing. Banding: ischaemic necrosis and fibrosis, then sloughing.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman has proctoscopy for painless rectal bleeding. Three engorged internal haemorrhoids are seen. The registrar records their positions on a clock face, described with the patient in the lithotomy position.
questions.q: At which positions are they most likely to lie?
questions.e: The three main anal cushions, and so haemorrhoids, lie classically at 3, 7 and 11 o'clock in the lithotomy position.

steps.x: The question asks: At which positions are they most likely to lie? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Three cushions, three classic positions.

elim: These are not the classic positions.
A single anterior lump is not the classic pattern.
These are not the classic positions.
6 o'clock is the classic site of an anal fissure.

steps.x: D: 3, 7 and 11 o'clock. Haemorrhoids: 3, 7 and 11 o'clock; fissures: 6 o'clock.
